items.prompt: How many jobs does a status update do at once?
choices: Two: it conveys accurate information and shapes trust in later updates
One: it reports the facts as accurately as it possibly can
Three: it informs the reader, persuades them, and apologizes
items.explanation: A status update is graded on accuracy and on whether the next update will be believed.

items.prompt: Draft A and Draft B were both true. What separates them?
choices: One of them contains a small factual error
Structure and specificity, not the underlying facts
Draft B is simply much longer than Draft A
items.explanation: The unit's whole point is that two honest drafts can differ in how much trust they keep, through order, specificity, and what they commit to.

items.prompt: What is optimism bias in a status update?
choices: Deliberately lying about progress to avoid blame
Always choosing the longest possible estimate to stay safe
Reporting the hopeful version as if it were the likely truth
items.explanation: It is not lying. Each update feels honest when written, but the pattern of unflagged hopeful dates reads as unreliable later.

items.prompt: 'Everything I said was true' defends which job?
choices: Only the accuracy job
Both jobs fully
Only the trust job
items.explanation: Truthfulness covers accuracy. Trust also depends on order, specificity, and frequency, which a true statement can still get wrong.

items.prompt: Which update fails the trust job even though its facts are right?
choices: 'Done and checked, as estimated last week'
'Should be done soon,' repeated after each miss
'One week late; the cause was a supplier delay'
items.explanation: A vague, repeated promise gives the reader nothing to check, so its accuracy cannot rescue its credibility.

items.prompt: Why does a vague update often cost trust only later?
choices: Readers dislike short messages on principle
Vague updates are flagged as dishonest immediately
The reader can only judge it once the vague claim fails
items.explanation: Vagueness feels fine until the outcome arrives; then the reader sees there was nothing to hold you to.

items.prompt: Trust in a status update is mostly about:
choices: Whether the reader expects your next update to hold up
How apologetic the writer sounds in each message
How many technical details each message includes
items.explanation: Trust is a forecast the reader makes about your future reliability, built from your past updates.

items.prompt: Maya says, 'I never lied, so why doesn't my manager believe my dates?' Best diagnosis?
choices: Her manager is being unreasonable about how estimates work
Her dates were vague and kept moving, which hurts the trust job
She should have apologized more warmly in every single update
items.explanation: Telling the truth satisfies accuracy. Repeatedly shifting, uncheckable dates fail the second job.

items.prompt: A contractor tells a homeowner every week, 'Kitchen's coming along, nearly done.' Each statement was true when said, yet by week seven the owner believes nothing. Best explanation?
choices: Each update was accurate but uncheckable, so only the trust job failed
At least one earlier update must have been an outright lie about progress
Homeowners distrust contractors whatever is said, so nothing could have helped
The weekly updates were too frequent for the owner to take in properly
items.explanation: Accuracy and trust are separate. 'Nearly done' can be true and still give the owner nothing to check, so repeating it spends trust.
items.reference:
Two jobs, one message
📋 Job 1: convey accurate information
🤝 Job 2: shape how far the next update is believed
❌ "I never lied" answers only job 1
Why: a true update can still lose trust if its delivery is vague, badly ordered, or silent.
items.learnMore:
Accurate is not the same as trusted

Accuracy asks whether the facts are right. Trust asks whether the reader will believe your next update. They are scored separately, and only the first is protected by simply not lying.

Common mistake

Treating "everything I said was true" as a full defense. It answers one job and ignores the other.
items.reflection: Think of a friend who is always 'five minutes away'. Every message may be sincere, so what exactly makes you stop believing them?

items.prompt: Which situation shows optimism bias rather than lying?
choices: The writer states a later date than they believe, in order to look safe
The writer reports 'done' for work they already know is still unfinished
The writer gives no date at all and says plainly that progress is unclear
Each week the writer sincerely repeats 'should be done Friday' with no new evidence
items.explanation: Optimism bias is sincere hope reported as likely fact. The other options are deception, padding, or honest uncertainty.

Only the second passes, because a longer explanation shows more effort made
Both pass the accuracy job; only the first reliably passes the trust job
Neither can be fairly judged until the whole piece of work is finished
items.explanation: Trust can be judged from how checkable and clear the update is, before the outcome is known.

Accuracy matters much less than sounding confident and calm to the reader

items.prompt: What does BLUF stand for?
choices: Be lengthy until finished
Bottom line up front
Blame, list, update, follow up
items.explanation: BLUF means the most important status or conclusion comes first.

items.prompt: In a delay update, what should come first?
choices: The full story of why it happened
An apology for the inconvenience
What is late and by how much
items.explanation: The impact is what the reader needs; the reason is context.

items.prompt: Why does leading with the reason read as an excuse?
choices: The reader must judge the justification before knowing the cost
Reasons are untrue when stated first
Readers dislike reading any explanation
items.explanation: Without the impact, the reader cannot tell whether the reason is good enough, so it sounds like a defense.

items.prompt: In BLUF, the reason is best treated as:
choices: A toll paid before the information
Context for readers who want it
Something to leave out entirely
items.explanation: The reason still matters, but it should not stand between the reader and the answer.

items.prompt: Does reordering sentences change the facts?
choices: Yes, order alters which facts are true
Yes, but only in written updates
No, only the reading experience changes
items.explanation: Same delay, same cause, same date. Only what the reader endures before the answer differs.

items.prompt: A reader waiting for the impact is mostly:
choices: Bracing for how bad the news is
Calmly weighing your reasoning
Checking the message for spelling mistakes
items.explanation: They cannot absorb reasoning calmly when they do not yet know the stakes.

items.prompt: Which opening is impact-first?
choices: 'Because the supplier changed their process, we ran into trouble.'
'This will miss today's date by one week.'
'I wanted to give you some background first.'
items.explanation: It states the status and size of the miss immediately.

items.prompt: BLUF is most useful for:
choices: Only good news, never bad news
Only written messages that run longer than a full page
Bad news especially, though it suits any update
items.explanation: Bad news is where readers brace hardest, so ordering helps most there.

items.prompt: A message reads: 'After the printer broke and then the courier lost the replacement, we reordered, so the posters arrive Tuesday instead of Friday.' Which rewrite best applies BLUF?
choices: Sorry for the trouble. The printer broke and the replacement was lost, so we reordered; posters should hopefully arrive Tuesday.
The posters will arrive Tuesday instead of Friday. The printer broke and the replacement was lost in transit, so we reordered.
Several things went wrong this week, starting with the printer; the posters will arrive Tuesday, later than planned.
The posters are delayed. Please bear with us while we work through a number of problems.
items.explanation: The correct version leads with the impact and a specific date. The others lead with apology or backstory, or give no date at all.
items.reference:
Same facts, different order
⬅️ Reason first: reader judges the excuse before knowing the cost
➡️ Impact first: reader gets the answer, then context
🎯 BLUF: bottom line up front
Why: order changes the reading experience even when every fact is identical.
items.learnMore:
Why the reader braces

Until they know how bad the news is, the reader is bracing, not listening. Putting the impact first ends the bracing, so the reason arrives as context instead of a defense.

Common mistake

Thinking a legitimate reason cannot sound like an excuse. Placed before the impact, almost any reason does.
items.reflection: Recall a time someone began with a long backstory before telling you what they needed. What were you doing with your attention while you waited?

items.prompt: Your manager asks directly, 'Why is the report late?' Which opening is best?
choices: The cause in one sentence, then the new date
The new date alone, ignoring the question asked
A long apology, then the cause, then the date
A request that they wait until you know more
items.explanation: The bottom line is whatever the reader needs most. Here they asked for the cause, so give it briefly, then the date.

Defensiveness comes only from word choice, and never from the order

The first message was a noticeably different length from the second
items.explanation: The reader reacts to the sequence: justification first reads as pleading, even with the same facts.

items.prompt: Which set lists the three things a believable update carries?
choices: A long apology, the full history, and a firm promise
A confident tone, a light joke, and a distant deadline
A specific estimate, a reason it is more reliable, and an explicit ask
items.explanation: These three give the reader something to check, a reason to believe, and clarity about what to do.

items.prompt: Which new estimate is specific?
choices: 'Finishing next Thursday'
'Soon, hopefully'
'In a little while'
items.explanation: A date can be checked later; vague words cannot.

items.prompt: Why does 'should be done soon' fail?
choices: It sounds too confident
No one can check later whether it held
It is always shorter than the reader wants
items.explanation: A claim that cannot fail also cannot build credibility.

items.prompt: 'Why this estimate is more reliable' means:
choices: How much effort you put in
How sorry you are about the miss
What changed since the last, missed estimate
items.explanation: A new guess needs a reason that distinguishes it from the old one.

items.prompt: Which line states an explicit ask?
choices: 'Nothing needed from you right now.'
'I hope that is okay with everyone.'
'We are all doing our best here.'
items.explanation: It tells the reader plainly whether they must act.

items.prompt: 'Falsifiable' means a claim is:
choices: Likely to be false
Specific enough that later readers can check it
Written in formal language
items.explanation: It is about testability, not about being wrong.

items.prompt: Staying silent about a previous missed estimate reads as:
choices: Confidence in the new estimate
Respect for the reader's time
Hoping the miss goes unnoticed
items.explanation: Readers remember the miss; ignoring it looks like avoidance.

items.prompt: Which claim is the most checkable?
choices: 'Finishing Thursday, once the last two items pass review.'
'Making good progress on all fronts.'
'Nearly there now, thanks for waiting.'
items.explanation: It names a date and the condition behind it.

items.prompt: 'The sofa will arrive on the 20th. The warehouse confirmed it is loaded on the truck, unlike last time when it was only listed as in stock.' Which component is missing?
choices: A specific new date for when the sofa will actually arrive
A reason that this date is more reliable than the last one
An explicit statement of whether the buyer needs to do anything
Any acknowledgment at all that an earlier date was missed
items.explanation: The date, the reliability reason, and the earlier miss are all present. Nothing says whether the buyer must act.
items.reference:
Believable versus eroding
📅 Specific new date, not 'soon'
🔎 Why this estimate is more reliable than the last
🙋 What, if anything, the reader needs to do
Why: each part gives the reader something to check, which is what vague updates withhold.
items.learnMore:
Checkable beats comforting

A claim is falsifiable when a later reader can see whether it held. 'Thursday' either happens or does not; 'soon' can never fail, so it also can never earn trust.

Common mistake

Believing 'soon' is safer because it cannot be wrong. It cannot be checked either, so it banks no trust.
items.reflection: Think of a plan you gave someone, such as a pickup time or a repair date. What would you have added to make them believe the second guess more than the first?

items.prompt: 'Sorry again for the delay! Things have been hectic, but I'm confident it'll be sorted very soon, no worries.' What is missing?
choices: Only the specific date; the reason and the ask are both present
All three: a specific date, a reason for confidence, and an explicit ask
Only the explicit ask; the date and the reason are both present
Nothing is missing; a brief and friendly tone builds the trust
items.explanation: Warmth is not a substitute. The message gives nothing to check, no reason to believe it, and no statement of what the reader should do.

items.explanation: A specific date is good; the issue is the missing reason it is better than the last one.

choices: 'Done by the end of the week, hopefully, if all goes reasonably well.'
'Done in roughly a few days, give or take, depending on the day.'
'Done well before the original deadline, as far as anyone can tell.'
'Done by Thursday noon if the review finishes today.'
items.explanation: It has a time, plus the condition it depends on. The others hedge without any boundary a reader could test.

items.prompt: A known claim is one that is:
choices: Verified rather than projected
Confidently worded
Likely to be true
items.explanation: Known means checked already, not merely expected.

items.prompt: An estimated claim should name:
choices: The person to blame if it fails
The assumption it depends on
The exact hour it was written
items.explanation: A named assumption makes the estimate checkable.

items.prompt: 'The fix is installed and tested.' This is:
choices: An estimated claim
A claim with no reader value
A known claim
items.explanation: It describes something that has already happened and been checked.

items.prompt: 'Testing should take two more days.' This is:
choices: An estimated claim
A known claim
A claim to remove
items.explanation: It projects the future, so it needs its assumption.

items.prompt: Why separate known from estimated claims?
choices: So the update looks longer and more thorough
So the reader knows how much weight each deserves
So you can avoid ever having to give a date
items.explanation: The labels carry the confidence level the reader needs.

items.prompt: Which sentence names an assumption?
choices: 'Posters by Thursday, I hope, all being well.'
'Posters by Thursday, give or take a day or so.'
'Posters by Thursday, assuming the printer has ink tomorrow.'
items.explanation: Only the first says what the date depends on.

items.prompt: When a named assumption fails, it gives everyone:
choices: A specific, checkable reason
Someone to blame
A reason to skip the next update
items.explanation: The failure traces to one condition rather than a vague sense of being wrong.

items.prompt: Blending known and projected claims makes:
choices: The update more honest
Every claim read with the same confidence
The reader more patient
items.explanation: The reader cannot tell what is solid and what is a guess.

items.prompt: 'The permit was approved Tuesday; the builders should start within two weeks.' How should this be read?
choices: Both clauses are known, because a permit exists on paper somewhere
Both clauses are estimates, because everything about the future is uncertain
The first clause is an estimate and the second is a known fact
The first clause is known; the second is estimated and needs its condition named
items.explanation: Approval already happened. The builders' start is a projection that depends on something, such as their schedule.
items.reference:
Label every claim
✅ Known: verified, state it plainly
🔮 Estimated: name the assumption it depends on
⚖️ Reader sets weight accordingly
Why: labeling tells the reader how much to rely on a number and gives a specific reason if it fails.
items.learnMore:
Why the assumption matters

A projection with its assumption attached is honest about its own limits. If the assumption breaks, everyone can point to what changed instead of concluding the estimate was just wrong.

Common mistake

Hedging with words like 'hopefully' instead of naming the condition. A hedge signals doubt without telling anyone what the doubt is about.
items.reflection: When someone gives you an arrival time, which do you trust more: 'about 6' or 'about 6 if the traffic on the bridge clears'? What does the second tell you that the first hides?

items.prompt: A teammate says, 'The migration is nearly done.' Which rewrite best separates known from estimated?
choices: 'The migration is nearly done and should be finished very soon.'
'Most of the migration is complete; what remains is mainly small details.'
'Nine of ten tables are moved. The last should finish tomorrow, assuming no new errors.'
'We are making good progress and do not expect any major issues.'
items.explanation: It states a verified count, then a projection with its assumption. The others stay vague about what is confirmed.

It would have turned the launch date into a certainty for readers
It would have made the whole update shorter and much simpler
items.explanation: Labeling does not change events. It makes the reason for a miss specific and honest instead of mysterious.

choices: 'The test run finished and all 40 checks passed.'

'The vendor says they will ship by Friday at the latest.'
items.explanation: A relayed promise is still a projection from your side. Only the finished test run is confirmed.

items.prompt: Why does update frequency matter?
choices: More updates always sound more professional
The reader judges how long they were left guessing
Readers prefer longer messages
items.explanation: Silence gets filled by the reader's own assumptions, which are rarely generous.

items.prompt: During real uncertainty, silence is usually read as:
choices: A sign of calm confidence
Respect for the reader's time
Either 'all is fine' or 'something is hidden'
items.explanation: Both readings are unintended and avoidable with a short update.

items.prompt: Compared with one surprise on the due date, small early updates tend to:
choices: Cost less trust
Cost more trust
Make no difference to trust
items.explanation: Predictability is part of trust, independent of whether the news is good.

items.prompt: Repeated vague misses:
choices: Each cost exactly the same
Compound, so the third hurts more than the first
Stop mattering after two
items.explanation: Each miss is judged against the ones before it.

items.prompt: In the unit's model, each vague miss removes:
choices: A fixed 10 points of trust
All remaining trust at once
40% of the trust that remains
items.explanation: The model is illustrative, not measured, and shows compounding.

items.prompt: An update with nothing new, sent only on schedule, trains readers to:
choices: Skim
Read more carefully
Reply faster
items.explanation: If every update looks the same, the important one gets skimmed too.

items.prompt: Which is a good short update during uncertainty?
choices: 'Nothing to report this week, no news at all.'
'Still investigating; next specific estimate by Tuesday.'
'Will send an update when I feel ready to share.'
items.explanation: It breaks the silence and commits to a checkable next step.

items.prompt: The rule behind update timing is best stated as:
choices: Always send an update every day, whatever has happened
Only send an update once the work is completely finished
Do not let the reader assume good news while you know it is uncertain
items.explanation: The test is what the reader is likely to assume, not a fixed calendar.

items.prompt: Using the unit's illustrative model (each vague miss removes 40% of remaining trust), about how much trust remains after two consecutive vague misses?
choices: About 36%
About 20%
About 60%
About 80%
items.explanation: 100 x 0.6 x 0.6 = 36. Subtracting 40 twice (20%) wrongly treats the loss as linear, and 60% counts only one miss.
items.reference:
Silence is not neutral
🔕 No news: reader fills the gap themselves
📬 Small early updates: delay feels managed

choices: It contained a deliberate lie

choices: Week 4
Week 2
Never

items.prompt: In Path B, when was the cause named?
choices: Week 3, after the midweek update
Week 2, on the original due date
Week 4, along with the final result
items.explanation: Path B led with impact and cause immediately.

items.prompt: What triggered Path B's midweek update?
choices: A fixed weekly schedule
The reader asking for one
New confirmed information

items.prompt: The claims chart counts:
choices: Total words written

choices: It scoped the real complexity early and set a realistic estimate

items.explanation: Honest early scoping gave the work a realistic target.

items.prompt: A caterer tells a client Monday 'menu nearly final,' Wednesday 'a few last tweaks,' and Friday explains that a supplier dropped out and gives a new date. Which pattern is this?
choices: Path B: cause and date named at the first miss

Neither; it is the ideal pattern for a long project
Path B, because the Friday message is specific
items.explanation: The earlier messages gave nothing checkable. A specific Friday message cannot erase two vague ones.

Each update is judged against the ones before it. A pattern of unchecked promises is what the reader remembers, not any single sentence.

Common mistake

Judging an update in isolation. Path A's week-4 'Friday' looks fine alone but inherits two broken promises.

choices: Strong accountability

items.prompt: Which is a brief, direct acknowledgment?
choices: 'This will miss the original estimate.'
'I am so incredibly sorry about everything that happened.'
'Mistakes were made along the way.'
items.explanation: It owns the miss in one clear sentence.

choices: Careful thinking

A request for patience
items.explanation: Neither reading is intended.

items.explanation: It breaks the silence and commits to a next step.

items.prompt: Which is a failure mode?
choices: Sending identical weekly updates with nothing new
Naming a cause on the due date itself
Saying plainly that nothing is needed from the reader
items.explanation: It dilutes attention and hides real news.

items.prompt: After the acknowledgment, the reader needs:
choices: More background on the past
The plan, the date, and the ask
A promise it will never happen again
items.explanation: These are the parts that help them act.

items.prompt: A message opens with four sentences of apology ('I feel awful, I know how frustrating this is...') and only then says the report will be three days late. What is the main problem?
choices: It is too honest about how the writer actually feels
It states the delay too bluntly for the reader to take in
The apology delays the impact and reads as managing feelings
It should have left the delay out of the message entirely
items.explanation: A single direct sentence handles accountability. Burying the date under apology makes the reader wait again.
items.reference:
Four ways good intent backfires
🙈 Staying vague to avoid alarm
🔁 Re-explaining with nothing new
🙇 A long apology before the plan
🔇 Silence mistaken for 'nothing to report'
Why: each one delays the useful information or teaches readers to stop paying attention.
items.learnMore:
Accountability is brief

A short, direct acknowledgment does the accountability work. The plan, the date, and the ask are what the reader still needs, and a long apology delays them.

Common mistake

Equating more apology with more responsibility. Past a sentence, it shifts the focus from the reader's needs to the writer's feelings.
items.reflection: When someone gave you bad news well, what did they do in the first two sentences? When someone did it badly, what did they do instead?

They should share every detail of the problem the moment it appears
They should say nothing at all until the slip has been fully resolved
items.explanation: Silence lets the reader assume the worst or the best. A short, honest update with a next date keeps trust.
